messages.author: bbcc6a39b583e937
messages.subject: Highly Correlated Posteriors and RM-HMC
parts:
I have a model with a posterior which is highly correlated and varies over the posterior.  I have attached a heatmap of a 2D slice of the posterior.

First, is if there is any hand tuning or specification through the "control" argument that can be done to improve STAN's performance on such highly correlated posteriors?  Should I expect NUTS to perform as well or better than HMC? I imagine using a dense mass matrix only makes matters worse?  Am I basically out of luck with such difficult posteriors?

Presumably this is where RM-HMC really performs well.  Is there any update on the status of RM-HMC?  

My problem is very similar to the section on unidentifiable models (section 2) in the discsussion of the RM-HMC paper here: of http://arxiv.org/pdf/1011.0057.pdf

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Highly Correlated Posteriors and RM-HMC
parts:
Thanks for the nice drawing --- that's the banana posterior
(Rosenbrock created a famous test case based on it that
Michael sometimes uses for illustration.)

Yes, a dense mass matrix is worse because the curvature
varies. The thing to do for NUTS is set a higher acceptance
rate target (adapt_delta) and a lower initial step size (stepsize).
That will force the Hamiltonian simulation to take smaller
steps and follow the curvature better. This is roughly the
suggestion that Luke Bornn et al. make in the comment on
Girolami and Calderhead's paper --- there's a critical step size
above which you'll have very bad approximations to the Hamiltonian.
Euclidean HMC and Euclidean NUTS just uses a first-order approximation
based on the gradient.

Yes, NUTS should do better than vanilla HMC.

Yes, RHMC (with geoNUTS, of course) should be even better.
Michael Betancourt has some wonderful animations relating to this.

We're hoping to get RHMC out some time soon (maybe in a few
months). All it's waiting on is us to sort out some of the
final issues with higher-order autodiff --- RHMC is already
implemented on a branch, it just won't work for general models
yet until the higher-order autodiff catches up.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Highly Correlated Posteriors and RM-HMC
parts:
Yeah, these kinds of shapes (especially if your posterior _really_ looks that
much like a banana) are indicative of multiplicative non-identifiabilities in
your likelihood, i.e. something like

y ~ normal(a * b, sigma);

in which case you’d want to sample from (a* b) directly and infer a and b
later.  If you can’t figure out from where in your model the non-identifiability
is coming then you have to wait for Riemannian, which means waiting for
the autodiff.

On Mar 6, 2015, at 4:11 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Hi, also if you understand the curvature well enough, perhaps you could introduce a transformation that would straighten it out?  I don’t think this would work in general and it probably wouldn’t work in your case either, but maybe it’s worth a try?

messages.author: bbcc6a39b583e937
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Highly Correlated Posteriors and RM-HMC
parts:
Thanks for the feedback! My posterior is not exactly Rosenbrock's posterior but looks very similar.  It's the result of unidentifiability from a non-ignorable missing data model.  A soft moment constraint effectively constrains the posterior to live on a D-1 dimensional manifold of R^D.  I want to specify subjective priors for the non-identifiable component of the model so I don't think I can easily transform the space / reparameterize.

I'll definitely try to adjust the adept_delta and stepsize parameters.

I'm excited for for RMHMC implementation!
